passage: The Class 10 board exams were four days away, and the power in Lalremsiami's part of Aizawl kept going off in the evenings. By candlelight she opened her science guide and instead started a list in her head: what if the paper was long, what if she blanked on chemical equations, what if she scored less than her cousin, what if the result ruined her chances of the science stream. An hour passed. She had read half a page. When Shalini called to ask how revision was going, Lalremsiami said, "I've been thinking about the exam all evening." It sounded almost like studying. But when she put the phone down, the guide was still open at the same page, and the candle had burned halfway down.

qa.q: How much had Lalremsiami read after an hour?
qa.a: Half a page.

qa.q: Why did "thinking about the exam all evening" feel almost like studying?
qa.a: Worrying about every way it could go wrong felt responsible and serious, so it seemed like preparation even though no revision was happening.

qa.q: What small step could Lalremsiami take the next evening?
qa.a: Set a short timer by the candle and revise just the chemical equations, noting any new worry on paper to come back to later.

qa.q: How might Shalini read Lalremsiami's answer on the phone?
qa.a: Shalini might assume she was revising hard, not realising the evening had gone to worry rather than study.

grounding: A teenager spends her revision time imagining every way the exam could go wrong, and barely starts studying.

passage: In their flat in Tolichowki, Rehana sat at her desk with the physics textbook open and her head full of the future. If she did badly in the pre-board, she wouldn't get into the good junior college. Then no engineering seat. Then Abbu's disappointment, and the neighbours asking. Every time she tried to start a numerical, another what-if arrived. By nine she had solved one problem. Her younger sister Zainab came in with chai. "You've been studying so hard," Zainab said admiringly. "I've been worrying so hard," Rehana corrected, half laughing, half near tears. "It feels like the same thing. It isn't." Zainab set down the chai and looked at the single solved problem. "Want me to time you for fifteen minutes? Just one chapter."

qa.q: How many problems had Rehana solved by nine?
qa.a: One problem.

qa.q: What does Rehana mean by "It feels like the same thing. It isn't"?
qa.a: She realises that worrying about the future feels as heavy and responsible as studying, but it has taken the place of actually doing problems.

qa.q: Which choice offered by Zainab could help Rehana start?
qa.a: A timed fifteen-minute session on one chapter, which shrinks the task and gives her mind something to do instead of worrying.

qa.q: How does Zainab see her sister's evening at first, and what changes?
qa.a: Zainab first thinks Rehana has been studying hard, then sees the single solved problem and offers practical help.

grounding: A teenager's worry about exams and her future replaces study, and her sister offers a short timed start.

passage:
"Varun, dinner. You've been in your room since four."
"Coming, Papa. I'm studying."
Nitin came into his son's room and looked at the desk. The maths book was open at the first page of the chapter. Beside it lay a sheet covered in writing.
"What's this?"
"Things that could go wrong in the exam." Varun didn't look up. "If the paper's long. If I get the calculus questions. If my pen stops. If I get sick. If I don't get into the science stream..."
"That's a long list."
"I need to be prepared."
"How many sums have you done?"
Varun was quiet. "None yet."
Nitin sat on the bed. "Worrying feels like work, beta. But the list isn't doing the sums. Let's pick the first three questions of the chapter. After dinner, together."

qa.q: How many sums had Varun done?
qa.a: None yet.

qa.q: Why does Varun say "I need to be prepared" about his list?
qa.a: Varun is anxious about the exam, and listing every possible problem feels responsible, as if imagining disasters is the same as getting ready for them.

qa.q: What choice does Nitin suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Doing the first three questions together after dinner, which turns the worry into a small, concrete action.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel seeing the long list and no sums?
qa.a: Nitin is likely concerned but calm, recognising that his son is anxious rather than lazy, and choosing to help rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager lists every way an exam could go wrong instead of studying, and his father steers him to three sums.

passage:
The week before my Class 11 chemistry unit test, I barely studied. That sounds lazy, but it didn't feel lazy. It felt like the opposite. I'm Deepika, and every evening I'd sit at the study table with the textbook open while my mind ran ahead: what if they ask the numericals I can't do? What if I blank on the periodic table? What if I get a low mark and Papa has to sign it? I thought, if I imagine every bad thing, at least I'm being careful.
By Thursday I'd done one page. My friend Farida came over and saw my notebook: a whole page of what-ifs, no equations. She didn't laugh. She just said, "Pick one what-if and study that." So we did numericals together for an hour. It was the first real hour all week.

qa.q: What did Farida see in Deepika's notebook?
qa.a: A whole page of what-ifs, no equations.

qa.q: Why did the constant what-ifs feel responsible rather than lazy to Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika believed that imagining every bad outcome was a way of being careful, so worrying felt like preparing even though almost no studying happened.

qa.q: What could Deepika try the next time the what-ifs start?
qa.a: Turn the biggest what-if into a task, like doing the numericals, and give it one focused hour, just as Farida suggested 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Farida to find a page of worries instead of equations?
qa.a: Farida could see a friend who was stuck rather than lazy, so instead of teasing, Farida offered a simple way in and studied alongside.

grounding: A teenager imagines every way a test could go wrong, which feels like being responsible but takes the place of studying until a friend helps turn one worry into work.

passage:
Tuition centre notes, Chetan sir, Class 12 physics batch, 3 February
Saurabh stayed back again today. He's bright and he works hard in class, but his practice sheets come back half empty. When I asked, it poured out: "Sir, what if the paper is lengthy? What if I get a bad centre? What if I don't clear the entrance and waste my parents' money?" He said he lies awake making lists of disasters and feels guilty if he stops, as if not worrying would be careless.
I told him his worry was doing a planner's job without actually planning. We took his biggest fear, a lengthy paper, and turned it into one action: a timed mock every Sunday. He wrote it in his diary. Next week I'll go through the first mock with him and see whether the sheets start to fill up.

qa.q: What action did Chetan and Saurabh turn the fear of a lengthy paper into?
qa.a: A timed mock every Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Saurabh feel guilty if he stops worrying?
qa.a: He feels that not worrying would be careless, as if the disaster lists are how he shows he takes the exam and his parents' money seriously.

qa.q: Why is a timed mock a better answer to Saurabh's fear than another list of disasters?
qa.a: It practises the very thing he fears, working against the clock, so it builds skill and confidence instead of only raising alarms.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's parents read his half-empty sheets if they didn't know about the worry?
qa.a: They might think he wasn't trying, when he was spending his energy on fear; knowing the truth could help them support him rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager lists every way an exam could go wrong and barely practises, because worrying feels responsible, until a teacher helps turn one fear into an action.
